cards.title: Seese’s conjecture
cards.formal: For every isomorphism-closed class C of finite simple undirected graphs, does decidability of its MSO\(_{1}\) satisfiability problem imply that some constant k bounds the clique-width of every graph in C?
cards.definitions: An MSO\(_{1}\) sentence is built from vertex equality, adjacency \(E(x,y)\), membership \(x\in X\) in vertex sets, Boolean connectives, and quantification over individual vertices and subsets of the vertex set. There is no built-in vertex order, edge-set quantification, parity predicate or other counting extension. For a fixed class \(C, Sat_{MSO_{1}}(C)\) consists of all finite encoded MSO\(_{1}\) sentences \(\varphi\) for which some \(G\in C\) satisfies \(\varphi\). Decidable means that one Turing machine, allowed to depend on C, halts and answers correctly for every input sentence. C itself is not an input to that machine; no complexity bound is required. By negating sentences this is equivalent to deciding the theory \(Th_{MSO_{1}}(C)\)={\(\varphi\): every \(G\in C\) satisfies \(\varphi\)}. A k-expression builds a labeled graph from single vertices with labels in \([k]\), disjoint union, relabeling every vertex of one label to another, and adding all edges between two distinct labels. The clique-width \(\operatorname{cw}(G)\) is the smallest k permitting such an expression after labels are forgotten; set \(\operatorname{cw}(\varnothing )=0\). The conclusion is \(\exists k\forall G\in C \operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\), with k depending on C. No hereditary, minor-closed, bounded-degree or finite-forbidden-subgraph assumption is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the implication for every such graph class, or give one class of unbounded clique-width together with a correct terminating algorithm for its entire MSO\(_{1}\) satisfiability problem. A single finite graph cannot refute a uniform width bound for a class. Model checking on a supplied graph, or decidability with a promise about sentence size, is not the premise. Results requiring parity predicates or restricted graph classes do not prove the full statement.
cards.why: A major proposed structural necessity for logical decidability, connecting graph decompositions, finite model theory and algorithms over infinite families of finite inputs.

importance.reason: A foundational conjecture asking whether bounded clique-width is unavoidable whenever an entire graph class has decidable vertex-set monadic logic.

progress.text: Seese establishes foundational connections between decidable monadic graph theories and bounded structural width, and formulates the conjectural MSO\(_{1}\) boundary.
Courcelle–Oum prove that decidable MSO\(_{1}\) with parity predicates implies bounded clique-width.
Dawar–Sankaran develop the antichain/minimal-hereditary-class reduction for the stronger grid-interpretation conjecture; preprint 2020, CSL 2022, journal volume 2025.
Mählmann characterizes bounded shrub-depth through logical expressiveness and records a stronger MSO-dependence conjecture that would imply Seese’s.
Duron–Mählmann–Toruńczyk prove bounded clique-width for hereditary 2-WQO classes; the hypothesis differs from decidability of MSO\(_{1}\) satisfiability.

references.locator: Posted 12 July 2026; v2 dated 26 July; hereditary two-label well-quasi-ordering hypothesis

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. Seese’s MSO\(_{1}\) decidability implication remains unresolved in the checked primary literature. The parity extension, the shrub-depth expressiveness characterization and the July 2026 2-WQO result have distinct hypotheses or conclusions.

context_blocks.text: An MSO\(_{1}\) sentence can describe a graph property by quantifying over sets of vertices. Three-colorability, for example, can be expressed by choosing three sets that partition the vertices and requiring each set to be independent. Checking such a sentence on one finite graph is always decidable by exhaustive search. The premise here is much stronger: from a sentence alone, decide whether it holds in at least one member of an entire, potentially infinite graph class.

Clique-width measures how many vertex labels are needed to construct a graph using a small repertoire of operations. Labels identify groups of vertices that receive the same future edge additions. Dense graphs can have small clique-width: a complete graph can be built with two labels by inserting one vertex, joining it to all previous vertices, and merging its label. Thus the conjectured structural restriction is not a sparsity condition.

The classical treewidth theorem provides the motivation. Seese proves structural restrictions from decidability of monadic theories, and the version allowing quantification over edge sets forces bounded treewidth. Grid-minor machinery supports that argument. The MSO\(_{1}\) conjecture replaces edge-set quantification by vertex-set quantification and asks for bounded clique-width instead. Transferring the proof requires a logical way of recovering the appropriate obstruction.

Bounded-width descriptions support decidability because graph properties can be translated into properties of construction trees. In particular, for each fixed k the full class of graphs of clique-width at most k has decidable MSO\(_{1}\) satisfiability. But the conjecture is only a necessary-condition statement for an arbitrary class C. One cannot infer that every subclass of a bounded-width class has decidable theory.

For a simple reason, such a converse would be false. Choose an undecidable set S of positive integers, and let C contain exactly the edgeless graphs whose numbers of vertices belong to S. All those graphs have clique-width one. A sentence specifying exactly n vertices would decide whether \(n\in S\) if satisfiability over C were decidable. Restricting which sizes occur can encode undecidability even when each individual graph has trivial structure.

Courcelle–Oum prove the implication after extending MSO\(_{1}\) with the predicate \(Even(X)\), saying that a vertex set has even cardinality. Their vertex-minor and isotropic-system machinery establishes bounded clique-width from decidability of this stronger logic. This strengthens the premise: a decision procedure for ordinary MSO\(_{1}\) sentences need not handle parity sentences. Therefore their theorem supplies substantial progress while leaving the exact statement here open.

Hereditary classes, which are closed under taking induced subgraphs, are a useful focus even though the card quantifies over all classes. If satisfiability is decidable on C, it is also decidable on its hereditary closure: ask whether some vertex subset induces a graph satisfying the input sentence, using a relativized MSO\(_{1}\) formula. Unbounded clique-width is preserved on passing to that larger class. Thus a proof covering all hereditary classes would suffice.

Dawar–Sankaran develop a stronger route through interpreting arbitrarily large grids. Their Theorem 3.2 reduces that stronger assertion to two settings: antichains of unbounded clique-width under induced-subgraph containment, and minimal hereditary classes of unbounded clique-width. They verify the grid interpretation for the known minimal families studied in their paper. This is a research program and collection of cases, not a completed classification of all such families.

The inherited ICALP 2025 paper by Mählmann settles a different boundary: on hereditary classes, bounded shrub-depth characterizes coincidence of first-order and monadic second-order expressive power. Its conclusion formulates a stronger conjectural relationship between clique-width and MSO dependence, explaining how parts of that conjecture would imply Seese’s. Shrub-depth and clique-width are distinct parameters, and a theorem about expressive power does not by itself decide satisfiability.

Duron–Mählmann–Toruńczyk’s July 2026 preprint proves that every hereditary 2-WQO class has bounded clique-width. Here 2-WQO means that every infinite sequence of graphs with two possible vertex labels contains an earlier graph embedding as a label-preserving induced subgraph of a later one. This resolves a related structural conjecture, but it starts from a well-quasi-ordering hypothesis. It does not turn an arbitrary MSO\(_{1}\) decision procedure into such an ordering property.

The unresolved implication asks whether decidable graph theories always have bounded constructional complexity. A proof would show that broad logical decidability cannot arise from some entirely different mechanism on classes of unbounded clique-width. A counterexample would reveal precisely such a mechanism. Either outcome would change how structural graph theory explains the limits of automated reasoning over whole families of finite structures.

references.title: Delineating Half-Integrality of the Erdős-Pósa Property for Minors: The Case of Surfaces
references.authors: Paul, Christophe; Protopapas, Evangelos; Thilikos, Dimitrios M.; Wiederrecht, Sebastian
references.locator: Conjecture 1; PDF page 3

cards.definitions: Graphs are finite, undirected and simple. A minor is obtained by deleting vertices or edges and contracting edges, with loops removed and parallel edges suppressed. An H-minor model in G consists of pairwise disjoint connected vertex sets B_v for v∈V(H), with an edge between B_u and B_v for each uv∈E(H); its support is their union. Let pack_H(G) be the largest number of models with mutually disjoint supports, and let τ_H(G) be the minimum number of vertices whose deletion leaves no H minor. The integral Erdős–Pósa property on C means that a function f:N_0→N_0 exists such that τ_H(G)≤f(pack_H(G)) for every G∈C. This one f may depend on H and C, but not on the individual graph. A class is minor-closed if it contains every minor of each of its graphs. A graph parameter is invariant under graph isomorphism and is minor-monotone when G′ a minor of G implies p_H(G′)≤p_H(G). Boundedness on C means one finite bound for all graphs in C. H need not be connected. No efficient evaluation algorithm or uniquely prescribed parameter is part of the conjecture.
cards.answer_criterion: The affirmative answer follows from the published finite obstruction-sequence characterization: for the target class of H-minor-free graphs, take p_H(G) to be the largest order of an obstruction in its fixed finite collection of increasing minor sequences that occurs as a minor of G, using 0 when none occurs. Minor monotonicity and the theorem’s excluded-sequence criterion give exactly the required equivalence.

cards.definitions: A graph is finite, undirected and simple. A graph class C transduces all graphs if there is one first-order formula φ(x,y), using adjacency, equality and a fixed finite list of unary vertex predicates, with this property: every finite graph H can be obtained by choosing G∈C, assigning arbitrary subsets of V(G) to those predicates, joining distinct vertices u,v whenever φ(u,v) or φ(v,u) holds in that colored G, and taking an induced subgraph isomorphic to H. First-order quantifiers range over vertices; φ and its predicate list must be fixed independently of H, while G and its coloring may vary. C is monadically NIP, also called monadically dependent, if no such φ exists. A k-flip of G partitions V(G) into at most k parts and independently complements or retains adjacency between each unordered pair of parts, permitting a pair to consist of the same part; loops are never added. The resulting graph has the same vertices. C is flip-breakable if, for every integer radius r≥0, there exist an integer kᵣ and a function Nᵣ:ℕ₊→ℕ₊ such that for every m≥1, every G∈C and every W⊆V(G) with |W|≥Nᵣ(m), there exist A,B⊆W with |A|,|B|≥m and a kᵣ-flip H of G for which dist_H(A,B)>r. Here dist_H(A,B) is the minimum shortest-path distance between one vertex of A and one of B, with distance infinity across components. The constants depend on C and r, not on G,W or m. No hereditary-closure assumption is required for this equivalence.
cards.answer_criterion: The affirmative answer is the published flip-breakability equivalence of Dreier, Mählmann and Toruńczyk, Theorem 1.3 in the full version. Its two directions exactly characterize all monadically NIP graph classes by a condition involving only graph partitions, adjacency changes, subsets and distances.

cards.formal:
Historical question, resolved affirmatively: is it true that for every hereditary class \(\mathcal C\) of finite simple undirected graphs,
\[
\mathrm{FO}=\mathrm{MSO}_{1}\text{ on }\mathcal C
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\mathcal C\text{ has bounded shrub-depth}?
\]
Equality of expressive power and bounded shrub-depth are defined below. The reverse implication was known in the original source; Mählmann’s published ICALP 2025 Theorem 1 establishes the full equivalence.

cards.definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph has a finite vertex set and a symmetric irreflexive adjacency relation \(E\). A graph class is closed under isomorphism. It is hereditary when, for every \(G\in\mathcal C\) and every \(U\subseteq V(G)\), the induced graph \(G[U]\) also belongs to \(\mathcal C\); this keeps exactly the edges of \(G\) whose endpoints both lie in \(U\).

First-order logic \(\mathrm{FO}\) uses vertex variables, equality, adjacency \(E(x,y)\), Boolean connectives and quantifiers over vertices. Monadic second-order logic \(\mathrm{MSO}_{1}\) additionally uses variables for arbitrary subsets of the vertex set, membership \(x\in X\), and quantifiers over those subsets. A sentence has no free variables. Both logics are interpreted on the graph itself, with no supplied vertex order, extra color predicates or auxiliary tree. There are no edge-set quantifiers in \(\mathrm{MSO}_{1}\).

Equality of expressive power on \(\mathcal C\) means
\[
\forall\text{ MSO}_{1}\text{ sentences }\varphi\
\exists\text{ FO sentence }\psi\
\forall G\in\mathcal C:\quad
G\models\varphi\iff G\models\psi.
\]
The sentence \(\psi\) may depend on \(\varphi\) and the fixed class \(\mathcal C\), but not on the individual graph. The opposite translation is automatic because FO is a fragment of \(\mathrm{MSO}_{1}\). No bound on translation time or on the length of \(\psi\) is part of this expressive-power assertion.

A tree model with \(m\ge1\) colors and depth \(d\ge1\) for a nonempty graph \(G\) consists of a finite rooted tree \(T\), a bijection from \(V(G)\) to its leaves, a color map \(\lambda:V(G)\to\{1,\ldots,m\}\), and a symmetric Boolean function
\[
F:\{1,\ldots,m\}^{2}\times\{0,\ldots,d-1\}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}.
\]
Every root-to-leaf path has exactly \(d\) edges. If \(u\ne v\) are leaves and \(h\) is the depth of their lowest common ancestor, then
\[
E(u,v)\iff F(\lambda(u),\lambda(v),h)=1.
\]
Symmetry means \(F(a,b,h)=F(b,a,h)\). The colors are labels for the representation, not a requirement that adjacent vertices have different colors. Depth of the lowest common ancestor is interchangeable with leaf distance because all leaves have depth \(d\).

The class has bounded shrub-depth when there exist fixed integers \(m,d\ge1\) such that every nonempty \(G\in\mathcal C\) admits such a tree model. Its tree, colors and function \(F\) may depend on \(G\); the same \(m,d\) must suffice for the entire class. The empty graph is included without a tree-model requirement. This harmless convention avoids a root-with-no-leaves exception and does not change boundedness. Allowing a separate number of colors growing with each graph would not be bounded shrub-depth.

The quantification is over all hereditary classes, without a decidability or effective enumeration assumption. This is a structural characterization of logical definability, rather than a running-time assertion for model checking.
cards.answer_criterion: The historical target is a proof of the displayed equivalence for every hereditary graph class under the stated graph signature and vertex-set semantics. In particular, necessity says that every hereditary class of unbounded shrub-depth has at least one MSO1 sentence with no equivalent FO sentence on that class. The cited published theorem supplies the missing direction.

cards.title: FO model checking on hereditary monadically dependent graph classes
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: For every hereditary effectively monadically dependent class C of finite simple graphs, do there exist a deterministic algorithm \(A_{C}, a\) computable function \(f_{C}:N\to N\) and a constant \(d_{C}\) such that \(A_{C}\) decides whether G satisfies a first-order sentence \(\varphi\) in time \(f_{C}(|\varphi |)(|V(G)|+1)^{d_{C}}\) for every \(G\in C\)? The precise effectiveness condition is given below; the graph is supplied without a structural decomposition.
cards.definitions: The class C is fixed, is closed under isomorphism and induced subgraphs, and is not part of each input. First-order sentences use equality, adjacency \(E(x,y)\), Boolean connectives and quantifiers over individual vertices. They do not quantify over sets, and no vertex order or arithmetic is supplied. The input is the explicitly represented graph G and the sentence \(\varphi\); the parameter \(k=|\varphi |\) is its encoded length. The algorithm must halt on every input, and its correctness and stated time bound are required when \(G\in C\); it need not recognize membership in C. To define monadic dependence, let \(\theta (x,y)\) be any fixed first-order formula using adjacency and finitely many additional unary predicates. A graph in \(T_{\theta}(G)\) is obtained by interpreting these predicates as arbitrary vertex subsets, putting an edge between distinct u,v whenever \(\theta (u,v)\) or \(\theta (v,u)\) holds, and taking any induced subgraph. C is monadically dependent when no single \(\theta\) gives all finite graphs among the outputs \(T_{\theta}(G), G\in C\). For an explicit effective version, define \(\mathrm{P}_{s}\) as the bipartite powerset graph with vertices \(a_{1},\ldots ,a_{s}\) and \(b_{S}\) for every \(S\subseteq \{1,\ldots ,s\}\), and edges \(a_{i} b_{S}\) exactly when \(i\in S\). Require a computable function \(b:N\to N_{\ge 1}\) such that, for every formula \(\theta\) and every \(G\in C, \mathrm{P}_{b(|\theta |)}\) is absent from \(T_{\theta}(G)\). Formula length includes its predicate symbols under a fixed effective encoding. This is the computable dependence-function convention of Mählmann’s Definition 12.24. The programs computing b and the eventual algorithm may depend on C; they are not extra per-instance certificates. The exponent \(d_{C}\) is independent of k. The query-evaluation problem here is for the plain graph signature; unary colours occur in the structural definition. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

cards.status_note: Explicitly open in the July 2026 neighborhood-complexity paper. The independent-side hardness and stable-side algorithm are known; radius-one merge-width does not provide the full algorithm. This card fixes the effective dependence-function convention to require a computable FPT bound. No resolution found through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: First-order logic describes many small graph queries with quantifiers over vertices. For example, the existence of a dominating set of size k can be expressed by choosing k vertices and requiring every vertex to equal or be adjacent to one of them. A direct evaluation can try \(n^{k}\) choices. Fixed-parameter tractability asks for the stronger form \(f(k)n^{d}\): the query may be expensive, but its length must not keep increasing the exponent of the graph size.

Graph structure can make this possible. The broad research programme asks which hereditary classes support such evaluation. Hereditary means that deleting vertices keeps a graph inside the class, a natural closure property when a query examines a portion of a database or network. Sparse graph classes gave early positive results, but dense classes with controlled structure also admit efficient model checking. Thus density alone cannot describe the boundary.

Monadic dependence measures whether unrestricted graph structure can be hidden inside a class through a fixed logical interpretation. Unary predicates mark arbitrary vertex subsets. A formula then defines new edges, after which selected vertices may be retained. If this process can generate every finite graph, apparently restricted inputs still contain arbitrary graph complexity in an interpretable form. Monadic dependence forbids that possibility.

The effective hypothesis matters to the exact computational claim. A structural class can have finite obstruction bounds at every logical complexity while those bounds grow faster than any computable function. Mählmann makes the dependence condition quantitative using forbidden powerset graphs and distinguishes computable parameter bounds from weaker conventions for fixed-parameter tractability. This card adopts that explicit effective formulation, so “there exists a finite bound” is not silently substituted for an algorithmically bounded parameter function.

One direction of the broader classification has been established. Dreier, Mählmann and Toruńczyk prove that first-order model checking is AW[*]-hard on every hereditary monadically independent graph class. Under the standard assumption \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{AW}[*]\), this excludes efficient model checking on the independent side. Their structural characterization uses flip-breakability, a separation property allowing controlled changes to adjacency between vertex groups. The missing direction is the algorithm for dependent classes.

A major positive theorem proves fixed-parameter tractability for monadically stable classes. Stability additionally forbids interpreting arbitrarily long linear orders; dependence forbids arbitrary graph encoding and allows more classes. The 2023 preprint by Dreier, Eleftheriadis, Mählmann, McCarty, Pilipczuk and Toruńczyk, published at FOCS 2024, settles the stable case using neighborhood complexity and suitable covers. It does not make the two structural notions equivalent.

Merge-width is a graph parameter used in existing model-checking theorems. Dreier and Toruńczyk describe a graph by a sequence of successively coarser vertex partitions, recording deviations from default adjacencies between parts. Their model-checking theorem applies to bounded merge-width when a witnessing construction sequence is supplied. This theorem assumes that a witnessing sequence is supplied and does not cover the stated input model.

The July 2026 neighborhood-complexity paper proves that, for every fixed positive \(\eta\), the number of distinct sets \(N(v)\cap A\) is \(O(|A|^{1+\eta})\) in a monadically dependent class, with the constant depending on the class and \(\eta\). It also constructs sequences witnessing radius-one merge-width \(n^{o(1)}\) in polynomial time. This supplies a concrete structural and algorithmic step. General first-order formulas require control at radii depending on the formula, so radius one does not complete the model-checking argument.

Related February 2026 work by Dreier and Kuske accelerates the construction of low-crossing orders and neighborhood covers, improving model-checking runtimes within the already tractable monadically stable setting. Such refinements are useful because they make the structural tools more practical, while leaving the dependent-versus-stable boundary in place.

sentences: First-order model checking asks whether a graph satisfies a logical sentence using vertex quantification and adjacency.
The conjecture seeks fixed-parameter tractability on every hereditary effectively monadically dependent graph class, parameterized by sentence length.
The structural promise limits which arbitrary graphs can be encoded through first-order interpretations with unary labels.

The reviewed formulation supplies no decomposition and requires a computable parameter dependence, so structural existence results or algorithms needing extra construction sequences do not automatically establish it.

cards.context:
First-order logic describes many small graph queries with quantifiers over vertices. For example, the existence of a dominating set of size k can be expressed by choosing k vertices and requiring every vertex to equal or be adjacent to one of them. A direct evaluation can try \(n^{k}\) choices. Fixed-parameter tractability asks for the stronger form \(f(k)n^{d}\): the query may be expensive, but its length must not keep increasing the exponent of the graph size.

Graph structure can make this possible. The broad research programme asks which hereditary classes support such evaluation. Hereditary means that deleting vertices keeps a graph inside the class, a natural closure property when a query examines a portion of a database or network. Sparse graph classes gave early positive results, but dense classes with controlled structure also admit efficient model checking. Thus density alone cannot describe the boundary.

Monadic dependence measures whether unrestricted graph structure can be hidden inside a class through a fixed logical interpretation. Unary predicates mark arbitrary vertex subsets. A formula then defines new edges, after which selected vertices may be retained. If this process can generate every finite graph, apparently restricted inputs still contain arbitrary graph complexity in an interpretable form. Monadic dependence forbids that possibility.

The effective hypothesis matters to the exact computational claim. A structural class can have finite obstruction bounds at every logical complexity while those bounds grow faster than any computable function. Mählmann makes the dependence condition quantitative using forbidden powerset graphs and distinguishes computable parameter bounds from weaker conventions for fixed-parameter tractability. This card adopts that explicit effective formulation, so “there exists a finite bound” is not silently substituted for an algorithmically bounded parameter function.

One direction of the broader classification has been established. Dreier, Mählmann and Toruńczyk prove that first-order model checking is AW[*]-hard on every hereditary monadically independent graph class. Under the standard assumption \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{AW}[*]\), this excludes efficient model checking on the independent side. Their structural characterization uses flip-breakability, a separation property allowing controlled changes to adjacency between vertex groups. The missing direction is the algorithm for dependent classes.

A major positive theorem proves fixed-parameter tractability for monadically stable classes. Stability additionally forbids interpreting arbitrarily long linear orders; dependence forbids arbitrary graph encoding and allows more classes. The 2023 preprint by Dreier, Eleftheriadis, Mählmann, McCarty, Pilipczuk and Toruńczyk, published at FOCS 2024, settles the stable case using neighborhood complexity and suitable covers. It does not make the two structural notions equivalent.

Merge-width is a graph parameter used in existing model-checking theorems. Dreier and Toruńczyk describe a graph by a sequence of successively coarser vertex partitions, recording deviations from default adjacencies between parts. Their model-checking theorem applies to bounded merge-width when a witnessing construction sequence is supplied. This theorem assumes that a witnessing sequence is supplied and does not cover the stated input model.

The July 2026 neighborhood-complexity paper proves that, for every fixed positive \(\eta\), the number of distinct sets \(N(v)\cap A\) is \(O(|A|^{1+\eta})\) in a monadically dependent class, with the constant depending on the class and \(\eta\). It also constructs sequences witnessing radius-one merge-width \(n^{o(1)}\) in polynomial time. This supplies a concrete structural and algorithmic step. General first-order formulas require control at radii depending on the formula, so radius one does not complete the model-checking argument.

Related February 2026 work by Dreier and Kuske accelerates the construction of low-crossing orders and neighborhood covers, improving model-checking runtimes within the already tractable monadically stable setting. Such refinements are useful because they make the structural tools more practical, while leaving the dependent-versus-stable boundary in place.

A positive answer would unify several major algorithmic graph frameworks through one logical condition and explain when small declarative queries can avoid repeated high-dimensional enumeration. A counterexample satisfying the effective hypothesis would show that the absence of arbitrary logical graph encoding is insufficient for tractability. Either outcome would sharpen the connection between graph structure and query evaluation.
